Items.Value: Is the hon. and learned Lady as concerned as I am about the backlog in the magistrates court, which is four times larger than that in the Crown court and growing at 16% a year, whereas the Crown court backlog is stabilised? If this really is a reform in the interests of efficiency, should she not be sparing the magistrates court at a time when their backlog is growing so fast?

I do not accept the premise of that question. I do not accept that we have a backlog in our magistrates court. What we have is a substantial caseload. The right hon. and learned Gentleman will know that the magistrates court hear more than 1.5 million cases a year, and it is coping well. What I do acknowledge is that we need to increase their capacity, which is why we are increasing the number of sitting days. In 2025 there were 114,000 sitting days, and we will increase that to 130,000 by 2028-29. 

	The other thing we are doing is increasing the number of magistrates. Under the previous Government, the number of magistrates in this country halved. We are going to restore the magistracy to its former glory. The changes that we have made to the application process, and the investment that we are putting into recruitment—quadrupling the budget—are already reaping the rewards, and we are on course to meet the 21,000 target. The right hon. and learned Member for Torridge and Tavistock (Sir Geoffrey Cox) is right to say that we need to grow capacity as we see a more expanded role for the magistracy, but I believe that we can do it and we are on track to do so. 

	We are reforming the automatic right of appeal. It is vital that there is a right of appeal, but it is also reasonable to ask a defence to identify grounds for appeal. By introducing a permission to filter out cases without merit, we will avoid a situation in which victims are needlessly put through unnecessary re-hearings where the appeal totally lacks merit. As I said, these reforms must be matched by the capacity to deliver them. That is why we are investing in our courts and in the people who make justice possible, and we remain on track to reach our target of 21,000 magistrates by 2028-29. We are also strengthening judicial capacity by boosting the number of district judges and legal advisers, who need to see better pay and career progression.

There remains a strong case for judge-alone trials in the small number of cases that pertain to complex and lengthy fraud and financial matters. I can confirm to the House that we will proceed with this measure, which has had strong support from those responsible for investigating and prosecuting serious economic crime. Our primary objective here is to minimise the burden on ordinary people, who sit as jurors on such trials. We know that these trials can be lengthy, often lasting months at a time, which can mean long periods away from work and family responsibilities, lost income and real pressure on family life.

We are clear that reform must bring down delays and improve victims’ experience. It must also command public confidence and protect the principles that have made our courts respected the world over. The destination has not changed—it has never wavered. We will provide swifter justice for victims and continue to pull every lever to bring down the backlog, so that people no longer have to wait years for their day in court.
